latin.118: Hac ratione sic proposita Theologorum auxilium sibi adjungit, & Vitakerum, Chamierum, Sixtum Senensem, & Bellarminum nominat. Nostros cur laudet non miror: ita enim in hac causa usuvenit, novitatis suspicionem amoliendi causa: Sed cur Pontificios? cur Bellarminum? Nosne putavit eorum autoritate moveri posse? Non arbitror: Sed suis rationibus conjungere voluit ad nos oppugnandos Bellarmini rationes. Eum enim dicit non contemnendis ad firmandam hanc sententiam rationibus fultum procedere in medium lib. 5. de Amiss. Grat. & Stat. pecc. cap. 18. Age igitur hujus etiam solvamus rationes, eoque majore animo quod si quid intelligo, receptae in Ecclesiis nostris doctrinae de peccato originali non obscure adversantur.
latin.119: Nisi ponamus, inquit, nos in Adamo, & cum Adamo vere peccasse, nulla ratione explicari poterit, quomodo in parvulis recens natis sit aliqua vera culpa, & hoc Catholicum dogma, non tam supra rationem, quam contra rationem esse videbitur. Antequam progrediamur, quid est in & cum Adamo peccare? Figuratam enim profecto locutionem esse oportet. Fortasse est nobis Adami peccatum imputari. Hoc posito, propositionem illam nego.
latin.120: Eam probat Bellarminus, Nam, inquit, quicquid dicamus in parvulis ex peccato haerere, sive reatum, sive aversionem, sive gratiae privationem, sive quid aliud; nullo modo parvulis vitio dari, ac ne esse quidem poterit, nisi processerit ab actione libera, cujus actionis illi aliquomodo participes fuerint. Nonne hoc est negare, vitium haereditarium, infantibus inhaerens, esse vere peccatum iis damnandis sufficiens, uti nostra pronunciat Confessio Artic. XI. Sed pergat. Nam primo, reatus, cum sit relatio consequens actionem, qui fieri potest ut existat in eo, qui non est particeps actionis? Valeret sane hoc argumentum, si nullum esset peccatum nisi actuale, nullus reatus nisi proxime actionem consequens. Nunc autem est etiam peccatum habituale, & reatus consequens habitum.
latin.121: Secundo (recito enim has rationes ut apud D. Garissolium extant) aversio habitualis, nisi praecesserit actualis, ne intelligi quidem potest. Hoc vero insigniter falsum est, si actualis aversio ipsorum parvulorum intelligitur. Alioqui quis negat aversionem actualem Adami praecessisse habitualem in ipso, & hanc esse in parvulos propagatam? Profecto aversio a Deo, in quocunque sit, hoc ipso quod est aversio a Deo, peccatum est. Tertio, fingamus parvulum aliquem habere aversionem & reatum, & tamen non peccasse cum Adamo, quis capere poterit, eum merito reprehendi, & puniri debere. Quam culpam habet in eo, quod ita generatus est? Num impedire potuit, ne sic gigneretur?
latin.122: Ex mente D. Garissolii peccasse cum Adamo est peccatum imputari, & quidem imputatione vitium inhaerens antecedente: alioqui nos istae rationes non oppugnarent. Jam autem sublata ista imputatione, potestne aversio a Deo, in quocunque sit, non digna esse reprehensione? Culpa quidem eius non est quod ita generatus est, sed quod ita comparatus est, quod nequam, quod impius, quod Dei adversarius est, haec est profecto magna culpa, non quidem, ut loquuntur, culpa actualis, sed tamen habitualis. Ab actuali inobedientia causa a qua est, extrinsece; ab habituali vero subjectum in quo est, intrinsece denominatur inobediens. Non est igitur parvulus reus ab actione proxime sed ab habitu: non quia malam aliquam actionem commiserit, sed quia ipse malus est, & ad male agendum comparatus.
latin.123: Quarto, non satis est ad culpam, ut aliquid sit voluntarium habituali voluntate, sed requiritur, ut processerit ab actu etiam voluntario; alioqui voluntarium illud voluntate habituali naturale esset, & misericordia, non reprehensione dignum. Immo inquam, id satis est ad culpam habitualem. Non enim vitium originale dicitur voluntarium, quia est a voluntate, sed quia est in voluntate: illo modo voluntarius est actus, isto habitus: Nimirum vitium illud est ipsius voluntatis malitia & pravitas, a qua, licet naturalis sit, mala dicitur. Quo magis autem naturaliter mala est voluntas, eo est pejor, & odio dignior.
latin.124: Caeterum quis non videt has rationes posse retorqueri? Reatus enim est relatio consequens actionem eius cujus est reatus, non autem alterius: & habitus sequi solet actionem eius cujus est habitus, non autem actionem alterius: Et, Num impedire potuimus, aut debuimus ne peccaret Adamus? Et, quomodo est voluntarium respectu voluntatis nostrae, quod tanto tempore, antequam ullam haberemus voluntatem factum est? Et, facit-ne illa imputatio, ut peccatum illud actuale Adami processerit ab actu voluntario nostro? aut sumus-ne minus necessario rei, quam corrupti? Num sumus commeriti, ut tales gigneremur? Legantur Theologi nostri, adversus vel Pelagium, vel Pighium, vel ipsum Bellarminum disputantes, praesertim cum tractant controversiam de peccato originali & concupiscentia, an sit peccatum, etiam post susceptum baptismum.

pass_a.118: With that reason thus set out, Garissoles joins to himself the help of the theologians and names Whitaker (Vitakerus), Chamier, Sixtus of Siena, and Bellarmine. That he praises our men is no surprise: so it is customary in this cause, to drive off the suspicion of novelty. But why the Papists? Why Bellarmine? Did he think we could be moved by their authority? Placeus thinks not: rather he wanted to join Bellarmine's reasons to his own to attack Placeus's side. For he says Bellarmine comes forward propped by reasons not to be despised for confirming this opinion, in book 5 On the Loss of Grace and the State of Sin, chapter 18. Come then, let us also dissolve his reasons — and with the more courage because, if Placeus understands anything, they are not obscurely adverse to the doctrine of original sin received in our churches.
pass_a.119: Unless we posit, says Bellarmine, that we truly sinned in Adam and with Adam, there will be no way to explain how there is any true guilt in newly born infants, and this Catholic dogma will seem not so much above reason as against reason. Before going on: what is it to sin in and with Adam? The phrase must be figurative. Perhaps it means Adam's sin is imputed to us. That being posited, Placeus denies that proposition.
pass_a.120: Bellarmine proves it: whatever we say sticks in little ones from sin — guilt (reatus), or aversion, or privation of grace, or anything else — can in no way be given to them as vice, nor even exist, unless it has proceeded from a free action in which they somehow shared. Is that not to deny that hereditary vice inhering in infants is truly sin sufficient for damning them, as our Confession pronounces in Article XI? But let him go on. First: reatus is a relation following an action — how can it exist in one who is not a participant in the action? That argument would hold if there were no sin but actual sin, and no reatus except what immediately follows an action. But there is also habitual sin, and reatus following a habit.
pass_a.121: Second (Placeus recites the reasons as they stand in D. Garissoles): habitual aversion cannot even be understood unless actual aversion has preceded. That is strikingly false if the actual aversion meant is the infants' own. Otherwise who denies that Adam's actual aversion preceded the habitual one in him, and that this was propagated into the little ones? Indeed aversion from God, in whomever it is, is sin by the very fact that it is aversion from God. Third: imagine some infant has aversion and reatus and yet did not sin with Adam — who can grasp that he is deservedly rebuked and ought to be punished? What fault has he in that he was so generated? Could he prevent being so begotten?
pass_a.122: In D. Garissoles's mind, to have sinned with Adam is for the sin to be imputed, and indeed by an imputation that precedes the inherent vice: otherwise those reasons would not attack Placeus's side. But once that imputation is removed, can aversion from God, in whomever it is, fail to deserve rebuke? The child's fault is not that he was so generated, but that he is so disposed — worthless, impious, God's adversary; that is truly a great fault, not actual guilt as they speak, yet habitual. From actual disobedience he is named disobedient extrinsically by the cause from which it comes; from habitual disobedience, intrinsically by the subject in which it is. So the infant is not guilty from an action immediately but from a habit: not because he committed some evil act, but because he himself is evil and disposed to do evil.
pass_a.123: Fourth: it is not enough for guilt that something be voluntary by habitual will; it must also have proceeded from a voluntary act — otherwise that habitual voluntariness would be natural and worthy of mercy, not of rebuke. On the contrary, Placeus says, that is enough for habitual guilt. Original vice is not called voluntary because it is from the will, but because it is in the will: in the former way the act is voluntary, in the latter the habit. That vice is the will's own malice and wickedness, from which, though natural, it is called evil. And the more naturally evil the will is, the worse it is, and the more worthy of hatred.
pass_a.124: Besides, who does not see these reasons can be turned back? For reatus is a relation following the action of the one whose reatus it is, not another's; and habit usually follows the action of the one whose habit it is, not another's. And: could we, or ought we, have prevented Adam from sinning? And: how is that voluntary with respect to our will which was done so long before we had any will? And: does that imputation make Adam's actual sin proceed from our voluntary act? Or are we less necessarily guilty than corrupt? Have we earned being begotten such? Let our theologians be read, disputing against Pelagius, or Pighius, or Bellarmine himself, especially when they treat whether original sin and concupiscence is sin even after baptism received. Stops before Garissoles's last reason from the imputation of Christ's justice.

118: With that argument laid out, Garissoles calls in the theologians' help and names Whitaker, Chamier, Sixtus of Siena, and Bellarmine. That he praises our writers does not surprise me: that is how this debate usually goes when novelty is the charge to be shaken off. But why the Papists? Why Bellarmine? Did he think their authority would move us? I do not think so. He meant to join Bellarmine's reasons to his own against us. He says Bellarmine comes forward on no contemptible grounds for confirming this opinion — book 5 of On the Loss of Grace and the State of Sin, chapter 18. Very well: let us answer those reasons too, and with the more spirit because, if I understand them, they cut plainly against the doctrine of original sin received in our churches.
119: Unless we grant, he says, that we truly sinned in Adam and with Adam, there is no way to explain how newborn infants bear any true guilt, and this Catholic dogma will look not merely above reason but against it. Before we go further: what does it mean to sin in and with Adam? The phrase has to be figurative. Perhaps it means Adam's sin is imputed to us. Take that reading, and I deny the proposition.
120: Bellarmine's proof runs: whatever we say clings in little children from sin — guilt, aversion, loss of grace, or anything else — cannot be vice in them, cannot even exist, unless it came from a free act in which they somehow shared. Is that not to deny that the hereditary blot in infants is truly sin enough to damn them, as our Confession states in Article XI? Let him continue. First: guilt is a relation that follows an act — how can it stand in someone who had no share in the act? The argument would hold if the only sin were actual sin, and the only guilt what follows an act at once. But there is also habitual sin, and guilt that follows a habit.
121: Second — I recite the reasons as they stand in D. Garissoles — habitual aversion cannot even be conceived unless actual aversion went before. That is strikingly false if the actual aversion meant is the infants' own. Who denies that Adam's own actual turning from God preceded the habitual turn in him, and that this was passed down into the little ones? Aversion from God, wherever it is found, is sin simply because it is aversion from God. Third: imagine an infant who has aversion and guilt yet never sinned with Adam — how is he justly blamed and punished? What is his fault in being born so? Could he stop being begotten that way?
122: On Garissoles's reading, to have sinned with Adam means the sin is imputed, and imputed ahead of the inherent blot: otherwise those reasons would not touch us. But once that imputation is set aside, can aversion from God, in anyone, fail to deserve rebuke? The child's fault is not that he was born so, but that he is so constitutioned — base, godless, God's enemy. That is a great fault indeed: not actual guilt as they speak of it, yet habitual. From actual disobedience he is called disobedient from without, by the cause that produced it; from habitual disobedience, from within, by the subject that bears it. So the infant is not guilty from a nearby act but from a habit: not because he did some evil deed, but because he himself is evil and set for evil doing.
123: Fourth: guilt is said to need more than voluntariness by habitual will; it must also have come from a voluntary act — otherwise that habitual voluntariness would be natural and fit for mercy, not for blame. I say the opposite: that is enough for habitual guilt. Original vice is called voluntary not because it comes from the will, but because it is in the will: the first way makes the act voluntary, the second the habit. That vice is the will's own malice and crookedness, and though natural it is still called evil. The more naturally evil the will, the worse it is, and the more hateful.
124: Besides, who cannot see these reasons turned back on themselves? Guilt follows the act of the person whose guilt it is, not someone else's; and habit usually follows that person's act, not another's. Could we — or should we — have stopped Adam from sinning? How is something voluntary with respect to our will if it was done long before we had any will at all? Does the imputation make Adam's actual sin proceed from our voluntary act? Are we any less necessarily guilty than corrupt? Did we earn being born this way? Read our own theologians against Pelagius, Pighius, or Bellarmine himself, especially where they ask whether original sin and concupiscence remain sin even after baptism.

118.decision: not for papal authority but to add his rationes to Garissoles's attack; Placeus answers because they clash with Reformed original-sin doctrine

119.decision: figurative; if = imputation of Adam's sin, Placeus denies the proposition

120.decision: Bellarmine's demand denies hereditary vice as true damning sin vs Confession XI; Placeus distinguishes habitual sin/reatus

121.decision: Adam's actual aversion preceded and was propagated; aversion from God is sin wherever found

122.decision: without that imputation, inherent aversion still deserves rebuke as habitual guilt

123.decision: enough for habitual guilt; original vice voluntary as in the will, not from a prior will-act

124.decision: same difficulties rebound on antecedent imputation; point readers to Reformed disputations vs Pelagius/Pighius/Bellarmine
